tema: The dancing plague of 1518 in Strasbourg
titulo: The 1518 Epidemic That Forced People to Dance to Death
hook: In 1518, city leaders tried to cure a mysterious outbreak by encouraging hundreds of people to dance themselves free of it.
descricao: In 1518, hundreds of citizens in Strasbourg began dancing uncontrollably until they collapsed from exhaustion. Was this strange outbreak caused by toxic bread, mass hysteria, or something unexplained?

versoes.rascunho: On July 14th, 1518, Frau Troffea stepped outside and began to dance. She couldn't stop, and what the city did to cure her only triggered a massacre. There was no music on that narrow cobbled street in Strasbourg. Yet her body convulsed frantically. Her eyes were vacant and expressionless. Within days, over thirty people joined her, thrashing their arms in total silence. City leaders panicked. Doctors believed their blood was overheated, and prescribed continuous dancing as the cure. So the council hired musicians and forced the victims to keep moving. It backfired horribly. Soon, up to four hundred people were trapped in motion. Up to fifteen dancers collapsed dead every day from heart attacks and sheer exhaustion. Victims wept and begged for help, but their legs refused to obey. Priests forced survivors into red shoes sprinkled with holy water, watching them dance until blood pooled in their soles. By September, the plague vanished. Scientists suspect moldy rye bread, while historians argue it was mass hysteria. Neither theory fully explains it. If your body suddenly turned against you, would you blame poison, or a curse?
versoes.editado: In 1518, city leaders tried to cure a mysterious outbreak by forcing hundreds of people to dance until they dropped dead. It all started on a narrow cobbled street in Strasbourg when Frau Troffea stepped outside in complete silence. There was no music, yet her body convulsed frantically, eyes vacant and expressionless. Within days, over thirty people joined her, thrashing their arms. Panicked doctors believed their blood was overheated and prescribed continuous dancing as the cure. So the council hired musicians, forcing the victims to keep moving. It backfired horribly. Soon, up to four hundred people were trapped in motion, with up to fifteen dancers collapsing dead every single day from heart attacks and sheer exhaustion. Victims wept and begged for help, but their legs refused to obey. Priests even forced survivors into red shoes sprinkled with holy water, watching them dance until blood pooled in their soles. By September, the plague vanished. Scientists suspect moldy rye bread, while historians argue mass hysteria, but neither theory fully explains it. If your body suddenly turned against you, would you blame poison... or a curse?
